title: Volume of Cubes and Cuboids
seo_title: Volume – Primary 6 Mathematics Worksheets with Answers (NERDC)
standard_text: Find the volume of cubes and cuboids; find a missing length; convert between cm³, m³ and litres; solve problems on tanks and containers. (summary of the NERDC Primary 6 Mathematics curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Primary 6 maths worksheets on volume: cubes and cuboids, missing lengths, litres and cubic centimetres, and water tank problems. 100 questions with answers.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height. Volume of a cube = side³.
  • If you know the volume and two lengths, divide to find the third: h = V ÷ (l × b).
  • 1 cm³ holds 1 ml, so 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre and 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.

Examples

Example

Tank 2 m × 1.5 m × 1 m

V = 3 m³

Answer: 3,000 litres

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding the sidesMultiply the three lengths.
Mixing cm and mUse one unit for all lengths.
Writing m² for volumeVolume is in cubic units.

c: the area of a football pitch

items.e: m³ measures volume, the space inside a 3-D shape, such as the water in a pool. Area is in m², length is in m and mass is in kg or tonnes.

items.q: How many cubic millimetres (mm³) are there in 1 cm³?
items.e: 1 cm = 10 mm, so a 1 cm cube is 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm = 1,000 mm³.

items.q: The volume of the cuboid is 300 cm³. Find the unknown height.
items.e: 10 × 5 × ? = 300, so 50 × ? = 300. ? = 300 ÷ 50 = 6 cm. Divide by both of the other lengths. Check: 10 × 5 × 6 = 300.

items.q: The volume of the cuboid is 168 cm³. Find the unknown breadth.
items.e: 7 × 6 × ? = 168, so 42 × ? = 168. ? = 168 ÷ 42 = 4 cm. Divide by both of the other lengths. Check: 7 × 4 × 6 = 168.

items.q: The volume of the cuboid is 240 m³. Find the unknown length.
items.e: 4 × 6 × ? = 240, so 24 × ? = 240. ? = 240 ÷ 24 = 10 m. Divide by both of the other lengths. Check: 10 × 4 × 6 = 240.

items.q: The volume of the cuboid is 240 cm³. Find the unknown height.
items.e: 12 × 4 × ? = 240, so 48 × ? = 240. ? = 240 ÷ 48 = 5 cm. Divide by both of the other lengths. Check: 12 × 4 × 5 = 240.

items.q: A cuboid has a volume of 1,080 cm³. Its length is 15 cm and its breadth is 8 cm. Find its height.
A cuboid has a volume of 840 cm³. Its length is 12 cm and its height is 10 cm. Find its breadth.
A cuboid has a volume of 600 cm³. Its breadth is 6 cm and its height is 5 cm. Find its length.
A cuboid has a volume of 2,100 cm³. Its length is 25 cm and its breadth is 14 cm. Find its height.
A cuboid has a volume of 2,160 cm³. Its length is 18 cm and its height is 8 cm. Find its breadth.
A cuboid has a volume of 1,728 cm³. Its breadth is 9 cm and its height is 12 cm. Find its length.
A cuboid has a square base of side 5 cm. Its volume is 200 cm³. Find its height.
items.e: Area of base = 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Height = 200 ÷ 25 = 8 cm. (5 × 2 = 10 is not the area of the base.)

items.q: A cuboid has a square base of side 6 cm. Its volume is 252 cm³. Find its height.
items.e: Area of base = 6 × 6 = 36 cm². Height = 252 ÷ 36 = 7 cm. (6 × 2 = 12 is not the area of the base.)

items.q: A cuboid has a square base of side 9 cm. Its volume is 324 cm³. Find its height.
items.e: Area of base = 9 × 9 = 81 cm². Height = 324 ÷ 81 = 4 cm. (9 × 2 = 18 is not the area of the base.)

items.q: A cuboid has a volume of 400 cm³. The area of its base is 80 cm². Find its height.
items.e: Volume = area of base × height, so height = volume ÷ area of base = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 cm. Check: 80 × 5 = 400.

items.q: A cuboid has a volume of 960 cm³. The area of its base is 120 cm². Find its height.
items.e: Volume = area of base × height, so height = volume ÷ area of base = 960 ÷ 120 = 8 cm. Check: 120 × 8 = 960.

items.q: A cuboid has a volume of 1,000 cm³. The area of its base is 250 cm². Find its height.
items.e: Volume = area of base × height, so height = volume ÷ area of base = 1,000 ÷ 250 = 4 cm. Check: 250 × 4 = 1,000.

items.q: A cuboid has a volume of 360 cm³ and a height of 6 cm. Find the area of its base.
items.e: Area of base = volume ÷ height = 360 ÷ 6 = 60 cm². An area is in square units (cm²).

items.q: A cuboid has a volume of 1,350 cm³ and a height of 9 cm. Find the area of its base.
items.e: Area of base = volume ÷ height = 1,350 ÷ 9 = 150 cm². An area is in square units (cm²).

items.q: A container has a volume of 1.2 m³. It is 2 m long and 0.5 m high. Find its breadth.
A concrete block has a volume of 4.8 m³. Its base is 2.4 m by 1.25 m. Find its height.
items.e: Area of base = 2.4 × 1.25 = 3 m². Height = 4.8 ÷ 3 = 1.6 m. Check: 3 × 1.6 = 4.8 m³.

items.q: The solid is made of 1-cm cubes. What is its volume?
items.e: One layer has 2 rows of 4 cubes = 8 cubes. There are 3 layers: 8 × 3 = 24 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too (only 18 cubes can be seen).

items.q: The solid is made of 1-cm cubes. What is its volume?
items.e: One layer has 3 rows of 3 cubes = 9 cubes. There are 2 layers: 9 × 2 = 18 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too (only 14 cubes can be seen).

items.q: The solid is made of 1-cm cubes. What is its volume?
items.e: One layer has 2 rows of 5 cubes = 10 cubes. There are 2 layers: 10 × 2 = 20 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too (only 16 cubes can be seen).

items.q: The solid is made of 1-cm cubes. What is its volume?
items.e: One layer has 3 rows of 4 cubes = 12 cubes. There are 3 layers: 12 × 3 = 36 cm³. Count the hidden cubes too (only 24 cubes can be seen).

items.q: Find the volume of the cuboid.
items.e: Volume = length × breadth × height = 11 × 9 × 3 = 99 × 3 = 297 cm³. Multiply all three lengths and write the answer in cubic units (cm³).

items.q: Find the volume of the cuboid.

items.q: Find the volume of the cuboid.

items.q: Find the volume of the cuboid.

items.q: Find the volume of the cuboid.
items.e: Volume = length × breadth × height = 10 × 8 × 11 = 80 × 11 = 880 cm³. Multiply all three lengths and write the answer in cubic units (cm³).

items.q: Find the volume of the cuboid.
items.e: Volume = length × breadth × height = 7 × 5 × 9 = 35 × 9 = 315 m³. Multiply all three lengths and write the answer in cubic units (m³).

items.q: Find the volume of the cuboid.
items.e: Volume = length × breadth × height = 12 × 6 × 3 = 72 × 3 = 216 cm³. Multiply all three lengths and write the answer in cubic units (cm³).

items.q: A cube has edges of 5 cm. Find its volume.
items.e: All the edges of a cube are equal: volume = 5 × 5 × 5 = 25 × 5 = 125 cm³.

items.q: A cube has edges of 8 cm. Find its volume.
items.e: All the edges of a cube are equal: volume = 8 × 8 × 8 = 64 × 8 = 512 cm³.

items.q: A cube has edges of 12 m. Find its volume.
items.e: All the edges of a cube are equal: volume = 12 × 12 × 12 = 144 × 12 = 1,728 m³.

items.q: A cuboid is 2.5 m long, 1.2 m wide and 0.8 m high. Find its volume.
A block of wood is 1.5 m long, 0.6 m wide and 2 m tall. Find its volume.
items.e: Volume = 1.5 × 0.6 × 2 = 0.9 × 2 = 1.8 m³. 0.9 m² is only the area of the base.

items.q: A container has a capacity of 4,500 cm³. What is its capacity in litres? (1 litre = 1,000 cm³)
items.e: 1 litre = 1,000 cm³, so divide by 1,000: 4,500 ÷ 1,000 = 4.5 litres.

items.q: A jug holds 2 litres 350 ml of water. What is this volume in cm³?
items.e: 1 litre = 1,000 cm³ and 1 ml = 1 cm³. 2 litres 350 ml = 2,000 ml + 350 ml = 2,350 ml = 2,350 cm³.

items.q: How many cubic centimetres are there in 1 m³?
items.e: 1 m = 100 cm, so a 1 m cube is 100 cm × 100 cm × 100 cm = 1,000,000 cm³. (1 m² = 10,000 cm², because area has only two lengths.)

items.q: Which of these is a volume?
items.e: Volume is measured in cubic units (cm³, m³). cm² is an area, cm is a length and kg is a mass.

items.q: How many litres of water can this tank hold?
A tank is 60 cm long, 45 cm wide and 40 cm high. How many litres of water can it hold?
A tank is 80 cm long, 50 cm wide and 45 cm high. How many litres of water can it hold?
The water in the tank is 20 cm deep. How many litres of water are in the tank?
items.e: Use the depth of the water, not the height of the tank: 40 × 30 × 20 = 24,000 cm³ = 24 litres (÷ 1,000).

items.q: The water in the tank is 35 cm deep. How many litres of water are in the tank?
items.e: Use the depth of the water, not the height of the tank: 60 × 40 × 35 = 84,000 cm³ = 84 litres (÷ 1,000).

items.q: The water in the tank is 28 cm deep. How many litres of water are in the tank?
items.e: Use the depth of the water, not the height of the tank: 50 × 25 × 28 = 35,000 cm³ = 35 litres (÷ 1,000).

items.q: 30 litres of water is poured into an empty tank. The tank is 40 cm long, 25 cm wide and 45 cm high. What is the depth of the water?
items.e: 30 litres = 30,000 cm³ (1 litre = 1,000 cm³). Depth = volume ÷ area of base = 30,000 ÷ (40 × 25) = 30,000 ÷ 1,000 = 30 cm.

items.q: 24 litres of water is poured into this empty tank. What is the depth of the water?
items.e: 24 litres = 24,000 cm³ (1 litre = 1,000 cm³). Depth = volume ÷ area of base = 24,000 ÷ (50 × 30) = 24,000 ÷ 1,500 = 16 cm.

items.q: 36 litres of water is poured into an empty tank. The tank is 60 cm long, 40 cm wide and 30 cm high. What is the depth of the water?
items.e: 36 litres = 36,000 cm³ (1 litre = 1,000 cm³). Depth = volume ÷ area of base = 36,000 ÷ (60 × 40) = 36,000 ÷ 2,400 = 15 cm.

items.q: A tank has a base 50 cm by 40 cm. 12 litres of water is poured into it. By how much does the water level rise?
Ali pours 27 litres more water into the tank. What is the new depth of the water?
A tank has a base 30 cm by 20 cm. It contains water 8 cm deep. 4.2 litres of water is added. What is the new depth of the water?
A tank has a base 60 cm by 30 cm. The water in it is 40 cm deep. 27 litres of water is drained out. What is the depth of the water now?
Water is let out until the water is 20 cm deep. How many litres of water were let out?
items.e: The water fell by 32 − 20 = 12 cm. Volume let out = 50 × 40 × 12 = 24,000 cm³ = 24 litres.

items.q: A tank has a base 80 cm by 50 cm. The water in it is 45 cm deep. 60 litres of water is used. What is the depth of the water now?
How many more litres of water are needed to fill the tank to the brim?
items.e: Empty part: 60 − 35 = 25 cm high. 50 × 40 × 25 = 50,000 cm³ = 50 litres.

items.q: A tank 40 cm long, 40 cm wide and 50 cm high contains 32 litres of water. How many more litres are needed to fill it completely?
items.e: Capacity = 40 × 40 × 50 = 80,000 cm³ = 80 litres. More water needed = 80 − 32 = 48 litres.

items.q: A tank 60 cm long, 30 cm wide and 45 cm high is empty. Water is poured in until it is 30 cm deep. How many more litres are needed to fill it to the brim?
items.e: The empty part is 45 − 30 = 15 cm high. 60 × 30 × 15 = 27,000 cm³ = 27 litres.

items.q: A tank is 60 cm long, 50 cm wide and 40 cm high. It is 34 full of water. How many litres of water are in it?
items.e: Capacity = 60 × 50 × 40 = 120,000 cm³ = 120 litres. 34 of 120 litres = 90 litres.

items.q: A tank is 50 cm long, 40 cm wide and 60 cm high. It is 25 full of water. What is the depth of the water?
items.e: The water fills 25 of the height: 25 × 60 = 24 cm. The length and breadth do not change.
